overview.title: Keras workflows and picking a backend framework
overview.chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras
overview.main_topic: Keras' spectrum of workflows, its pluggable backends (JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch), the layered stack of Figure 3.4, and how to choose a backend
overview.central_idea: Keras is a high-level API sitting on a pluggable low-level backend (TensorFlow, PyTorch or JAX), which in turn runs on CPU, GPU or TPU. Because backends can be swapped after the code is written, you can debug, train and deploy the same model with different frameworks. TensorFlow is the default; you change it, for example, with the KERAS_BACKEND environment variable.
overview.importance: Backend selection is the first practical setup step for all Keras code in the book, and it must happen before Keras is imported.
learning_objectives: Explain why Keras supports many workflows rather than one 'true' way
Describe the three-layer stack of Figure 3.4 and what each layer is responsible for
Explain what 'pluggable backends' means and give the book's debug/train/deploy example
Know the default backend and how to switch it with KERAS_BACKEND
prerequisites: Basics of TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX (sections 3.3–3.5)
The high-level vs low-level distinction between Keras and the other frameworks (p.87)

summary:
The page finishes the list of Keras users (Waymo uses Keras models to process sensor data, and Keras is popular on **Kaggle**). It then draws a design consequence. Because the user base is diverse, Keras **doesn't force a single "true" way** of building and training models. It offers a **spectrum of workflows from very high-level to very low-level**, with several ways to build models and several ways to train them, each a trade-off between **usability and flexibility**. Chapter 7 covers much of this spectrum.

Section **3.6.1, First steps with Keras**, starts with configuration that must be done *before* Keras is imported.

**Picking a backend framework.** Keras runs on **JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch**, its "backend frameworks". Through them it can run on GPU, TPU or CPU, scale to thousands of machines, and deploy to many platforms. **Figure 3.4** shows the stack:

- **Keras** on top, for deep learning development: layers, models, optimizers, losses, metrics, training loops;
- the **backend framework** in the middle, the tensor manipulation infrastructure: tensors, variables, automatic differentiation, distribution;
- **hardware** (CPU, GPU, TPU) at the bottom, which does the execution.

Backends are **pluggable**. You can switch backend *after* writing Keras code, so you aren't locked into one ecosystem. The authors' example is to debug a model with PyTorch, train it on TPU with JAX for maximum efficiency, then run inference with TensorFlow's tooling.

The **default backend is TensorFlow**: a plain `import keras` in a fresh environment runs on TensorFlow. There are two ways to change it. The first, begun on this page, is the environment variable **`KERAS_BACKEND`**, e.g. `export KERAS_BACKEND=jax` before starting Python. Setting it from inside a script, and the `~/.keras/keras.json` config file, are covered on p.116.

concepts.name: Keras backend framework
concepts.definition: The low-level tensor-computing platform (JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch) that Keras uses to run its computations.
concepts.intuition: Keras is the steering wheel and dashboard; the backend is the engine. You can swap engines and keep driving the same way.
concepts.technical: The backend provides tensors, variables, autodiff and distribution, and maps operations onto CPU, GPU or TPU. It is selected at import time through KERAS_BACKEND or ~/.keras/keras.json. The default is TensorFlow.
concepts.significance: It lets one Keras codebase use each framework's strengths at different stages of a project.
concepts.example: Debug with PyTorch, train on TPU with JAX, serve with TensorFlow (book's example).
concepts.misconception: You cannot reliably change the backend in a running session after `import keras`. It must be set before the import.

concepts.name: Spectrum of workflows
concepts.definition: Keras offers many ways to build and train models, from very high-level to very low-level, each trading usability for flexibility.
concepts.intuition: It works like a camera with an automatic mode and a full manual mode.
concepts.technical: Model building ranges from Sequential and Functional models to subclassing. Training ranges from fit() to a custom train_step to fully custom loops. Chapter 7 reviews them.
concepts.significance: Different users (researchers, engineers, hobbyists) can work at the level they need.
concepts.example: A hobbyist uses `model.fit()`; a researcher writes a custom JAX training step with stateless_call (p.242).
concepts.misconception: High-level and low-level Keras are not separate libraries. They are layers of the same API and can be mixed.

code.title: Selecting JAX as the backend from the shell (inline in text)
code.what_it_does: Sets the environment variable KERAS_BACKEND to 'jax' in the current shell, so Python processes started afterwards import Keras with the JAX backend.

line_explanations.explanation: `export` makes the variable visible to child processes, such as the python REPL you launch next.

code.inputs_outputs: No output. It changes the environment of later processes.
code.algorithm: When imported, Keras checks KERAS_BACKEND (then the config file, then the default) to decide which backend to load.
code.theory_link: This implements the pluggable-backend idea of Figure 3.4.
pitfalls: It must be set before Python starts (or, for the in-code variant on p.116, before the first import keras).
Beyond the book: on Windows cmd the equivalent is `set KERAS_BACKEND=jax`; `export` is POSIX-shell syntax.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written check of which backend is active
import keras
print(keras.backend.backend())  # e.g. 'jax'

deeper.title: Matching backend strengths to project stages
deeper.body:
The book's example, read against the 'what makes X unique' sections:

| Stage | Backend | Why (from the book) |
|---|---|---|
| Debug | PyTorch | Eager by default, so easy to inspect (p.105) |
| Train on TPU | JAX | Fastest for most models, built for XLA/TPUs (p.114) |
| Inference / deployment | TensorFlow | Most mature production deployment ecosystem (p.98) |

The table layout is ours; the reasons come from the pages cited.

deeper.title: Resolution order for the backend setting
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a description of Keras 3 behaviour:
1. If `KERAS_BACKEND` is set in the environment when `keras` is imported, it wins.
2. Otherwise Keras reads `"backend"` from `~/.keras/keras.json` (created on first import).
3. Otherwise it falls back to the default, TensorFlow.

Because this happens at import time, changing the setting requires a fresh Python process or kernel.

misconceptions.claim: Keras is part of TensorFlow and only runs on TensorFlow.
misconceptions.correction: TensorFlow is only the default backend. Keras can run on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, and they are pluggable.

misconceptions.claim: You must choose a backend before writing any model code and are locked in afterwards.
misconceptions.correction: The book stresses you can switch backend after writing Keras code and move models between frameworks.

misconceptions.claim: Keras has one recommended way of building and training models.
misconceptions.correction: It deliberately offers a spectrum of workflows trading usability against flexibility (chapter 7).

misconceptions.claim: Setting KERAS_BACKEND after import keras changes the backend.
misconceptions.correction: The backend is fixed when Keras is imported; set it before (p.116).

takeaways: Keras offers a spectrum of workflows trading usability for flexibility; chapter 7 explores it.
Keras runs on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch, which handle tensors, variables, autodiff and distribution on CPU, GPU or TPU.
Backends are pluggable: the same Keras code can be debugged, trained and deployed with different frameworks.
TensorFlow is the default backend; change it with KERAS_BACKEND (e.g. export KERAS_BACKEND=jax) before importing Keras.

questions.question: In Figure 3.4, which tier is responsible for automatic differentiation?
questions.explanation: The figure lists tensors, variables, automatic differentiation and distribution next to the backend framework. Keras handles layers, models, losses and so on, and hardware only executes. The OS is not in the figure.

questions.question: What backend does `import keras` use in a fresh, unconfigured environment?
questions.explanation: The page says the default backend right now is TensorFlow.

questions.question: Using the book's example, explain why being able to switch backends after writing code is useful.
questions.answer: Each framework has different strengths. You can debug with PyTorch (eager, easy to inspect), train on TPU with JAX (maximum efficiency), and run inference with TensorFlow's deployment tooling, all with the same model code.
questions.explanation: This is the example given in the 'pluggable' paragraph, combined with the strengths listed in 3.3.3, 3.4.3 and 3.5.5.

questions.question: Why does Keras provide many workflows instead of one?
options: Because different backends require different APIs
Because its diverse user base needs different trade-offs between usability and flexibility
Because Keras 3 kept every legacy API for backward compatibility
Because high-level workflows are slower and must be avoided in production
questions.answer: Because its diverse user base needs different trade-offs between usability and flexibility
questions.explanation: That is the stated reason. The workflows are backend-agnostic, not tied to specific backends. Legacy compatibility isn't the stated motive, and nothing on the page says high-level workflows must be avoided.

questions.question: Write the shell command the book gives to use JAX as the Keras backend.
questions.explanation: Run it before starting the Python REPL.

questions.answer: Keras: e.g. layers, models, optimizers, losses, metrics, training loops. Backend: tensors, variables, autodiff, distribution. Hardware: execution on CPU/GPU/TPU.
